messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'd like to embed an R graphics device in a java swing application using JRI
and JavaGD.  I've looked at the JGR code a bit and yet I don't see how or
where the graphics device is set up.

Suppose for instance I wanted to display a plot (e.g. plot(1:10)) in a java
application using the JGDBufferedPanel class.  How do I register a JavaGD
instance with R?  How does JGDBufferedPanel discover this instance (or how
does R discover the JGDBufferedPanel instance)?

An outline of the steps required to get the barest possible java swing
application using JRI/JavaGD would be very helpful (or  a pointer to the
place to look in JGR source).

thanks very much,

Brad Buchsbaum

I'm not sure what you mean - JavaGD is the device so you simply use  
the device (you don't register any "instances" - whatever you mean by  
that). The only custom setting you have to touch if you don't want the  
default JavaGD class is to set JAVAGD_CLASS_NAME env.var to your class  
name (see the http://rforge.net/JavaGD/).


> An outline of the steps required to get the barest possible java  
> swing application using JRI/JavaGD would be very helpful (or  a  
> pointer to the place to look in JGR source).

Either take org.rosuda.javaGD.JavaGD sources from JavaGD and replace  
Frame->JFrame, GDCanvas->JGDBufferedPanel or take  
org.rosuda.JGR.toolkit.JavaGD form JGR, replace TJFrame->JFrame and  
remove the EzMenu stuff.

Cheers,
Simon

Hello,

I will have a closer look later, but one thing I can spot right now is 
that the code below is wrong :

		//Empty the environment...
                 execute(engine, "rm(list=ls())", environment);

You need to use arguments envir of ls and rm.

clear <- function( env = globalenv() ){
	rm( ls( envir = ls() ),  envir = env )
}

otherwise you remove all objects in the global environment.

What you do looks like this :

 > e <- new.env()
 > e[["x"]] <- 2
 > e[["y"]] <- 3
 > eval( rm(list=ls()), envir = e )
Error in eval(rm(list = ls()), envir = e) : object 'e' not found

where you should do this :

 > e <- new.env()
 > e[["x"]] <- 2
 > e[["y"]] <- 3
 > rm( list=ls(envir=e), envir=e)

It would be nice to have some more methods in REXPEnvironment to deal 
with this.

Romain

The really funny thing is that R has no API for removing an entry form  
an environment -- there is no other way to remove a variable from an  
environment than to use eval(LCONS(install("rm"), ...)). That is the  
reason why REngine has no method for removing a variable... Hence  
eval("rm(...)") is in fact the most effective way to do this.

BTW: looking at Fabio's test code it is invalid -- you cannot call  
close() and the createEngine() with JRI because R does not support re- 
initialization. (Aside from the fact that this is not even how you're  
supposed to use this! You should either use the JRIEngine constructor  
(if you want to tie your application specifically to JRI) or REngine  
factory (if you want your application to be backend-agnostic) -- see  
the supplied examples.

Cheers,
Simon

using the "round trip to R" method:

bool Environment::remove( const std::string& name) throw(binding_is_locked){
     	    if( exists(name) ){
     	    	    if( bindingIsLocked(name) ){
     	    	    	    throw binding_is_locked(name) ;
     	    	    } else{
     	    	    	    /* unless we want to copy all of do_remove,
     	    	    	       we have to go back to R to do this operation */
     	    	    	    SEXP call = Rf_lang2(
     	    	    	    	    Rf_install( ".Internal" ),
     	    	    	    	    Rf_lcons( Rf_install( "remove" ),
     	    	    	    	    	    Rf_cons( Rf_mkString(name.c_str()),
     	    	    	    	    	    	    Rf_cons( m_sexp,
     	    	    	    	    	    	    	    Rf_cons( Rf_ScalarLogical( FALSE 
), R_NilValue )
     	    	    	    	    	    	    	    )

     	    	    	    	    ) ;

     	    	    }
     	    } else{
     	    	throw no_such_binding(name) ;
     	    }

Quoted identifiers are part of the SQL standard.  They are supported
by virtually every common database.  It is a problem because the way
RJDBC works now column names get converted to upper case.

In the standard quoted identifiers are called delimited identifiers.
Also note that there is an RJDBC  identifier.quote argument that could
be used to specify which one to be used (normally it would be " or '
).

RJDBC's dbWriteTable is generating this string (wrong):

    "CREATE TABLE BOD (Time DOUBLE PRECISION,demand DOUBLE PRECISION)"

whereas RSQLite's dbWriteTable (and presumably also RMySQL) generate
this string (correct for sqlite):

   "CREATE TABLE `BOD` \n( \"Time\" REAL,\n\tdemand REAL \n)"

where its the lack of quoting of the names in the first string that is
the problem.

In fact the way I found this problem was in trying to convert a short
test RSQLite based program to one based on RJDBC/H2 and expected it to
work out of the box since that is the whole idea of DBI and it almost
did work but the dbWriteTable problem prevented transparent
conversion.

The thread is about the undesirability of global options and that this
problem is lessened if the option can be explicitly passed in an
argument so that you can be sure of the result without reliance on the
global parameters.

Thus it would be better if we could write:

myfn2 <- function(...args..., java.parameters = "-Dparam=value") {
   ...
   JDBC(...args..., java.parameters = java.parameters)
   ...
}

Rather than

myfn <- function(...,args..., java.parameters = "-Dparam=value") {
   ...
   options(java.parameters = java.parameters)
   JDBC(...args...)
   ...
}

Note that this still leaves open the possibility to use global
parameters which can be convenient at times even if dangerous but it
also provides the ability to work without them.

Before this spirals, I'll just help with a few facts from the sidelines.

Rosuda.JGR does generate a JGRError.log, see http://www.rforge.net/org/docs/org/rosuda/JGR/util/ErrorMsg.html  

Dropbox (https://www.dropbox.com/) is an amazingly useful program which allows files to sync across machines, and across people, 1st 2gb shared folderspace is free!.   So, I could have a dropbox sync files from my home to my work machine, and also share that with Simon, so we could all have a shared folder kept up to sync on multiple machines.

However, it struggles with rapidly updating files (say, an Outlook mailbox file) so if a program either holds a file open and constantly updates it, or if a program opens and closes a file rapidly, that can cause problems as Dropbox tries to sync the files.  This can cause conflicts and errors in the programs trying to access the data.

Michael (you don't remember me, but we met back when I was in Social Psych at UNC, and I was UVa undergrad): Dropbox is awesome, but you really need to test different apps with it.  I've had all kinds of innocuous apps choke when faced with Dropbox updates.   I hate to say it, but you may find that you can't rely on the live sync but instead have to copy files out when working with them, then updating a master copy when you have finalized your thoughts and chnages.  I know that sort of defeats the purpose, but it's where you may be.

The guys at Dropbox are pretty good at helping to think through these things, so when you figure out what type of file activity is generating the issues, they may have a workaround. 

If I recall, Michael, you are a mac guy, but my windows pals also like Microsoft's Live Mesh, which is 5gb free, similar functionality, but not as rapid updating and I dont' recall if it supports Mac at this point; could be a workaround to examine.

Best, and thanks to all for the awesome JGR system,

Michael Wexler
